The proposed answer is wrong. The correct count is $3^{2025}$, not $2^{2025}$.

**Where the proposal fails.** It assumes each brick in layer $n$ touches exactly two bricks in layer $n+1$. The row lengths don't allow this. Layer $n$ has $N=2^n-1$ bricks and layer $n+1$ has $2N+1$, so a brick of layer $n$ is slightly more than twice as wide as a brick of layer $n+1$ and overlaps three bricks below it.

**Adjacency.** Measure the wall as $[0,1]$. Brick $i$ of layer $n$ covers $[i/N,(i+1)/N]$, and brick $j$ of layer $n+1$ covers $[j/(2N+1),(j+1)/(2N+1)]$. Two bricks share a side exactly when their open intervals overlap. Scaling by $N(2N+1)$, this gives
$$jN < (i+1)(2N+1) \quad\text{and}\quad (j+1)N > i(2N+1).$$
Using $0\le i\le N-1$, these reduce to $2i \le j \le 2i+2$. So brick $i$ in layer $n$ connects to bricks $2i$, $2i+1$, $2i+2$ in layer $n+1$.

**Check on small layers.** Layer 1 has one brick and it overlaps all three bricks of layer 2. Layer 2 brick 1 spans $[1/3,2/3]$ and overlaps bricks 2, 3, 4 of layer 3 (which spans $[j/7,(j+1)/7]$), matching $2i,2i+1,2i+2$.

**Boundary.** If $i\le N-1$, then $2i+2\le 2N = N_{n+1}-1$, so all three choices always exist. Every move therefore has exactly 3 options regardless of history, and distinct choices lead to distinct bricks.

**Count.** Jessica makes $2026-1=2025$ moves, each with 3 choices. The number of distinct move sequences is $3^{2025}$. Direct enumeration confirms $3$ paths to layer 2 and $9$ to layer 3.

The given numerical value is approximately $3.85\times10^{609}$, which matches $2^{2025}$, not $3^{2025}$. Since $3^{2025}\approx10^{966}$, the stated answer is incorrect.

VERDICT: REJECT
